title: Finite discrete deterministic systems must eventually repeat

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Finite discrete deterministic systems must eventually repeat

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Any system of limited size made of discrete elements and following definite rules must eventually exhibit repetitive behavior, with repetition period at most equal to its total number of possible states.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: it is then a general result that any system of limited size that involves discrete elements and follows definite rules must always eventually exhibit repetitive behavior.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 6, “Starting from Randomness”; section “Systems of Limited Size and Class 2 Behavior” (from p. 255), p. 255. Scope: finite-state deterministic discrete systems

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The claim is an elementary theorem for finite deterministic state spaces. Its assumptions and bound are exact, and a short proof resolves the full scope.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Apply the pigeonhole principle to the deterministic trajectory through N possible states: within N+1 visited states one repeats, after which determinism forces a cycle of period at most N.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The claim is the pigeonhole principle on a finite deterministic state set: after at most N steps a state recurs, and the period is then at most N. The argument matches the full stated scope and can be checked in an afternoon. No external dataset enters, because the state set is the entire input to the proof.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: A deterministic system with N states follows a path in a finite set, so some state repeats by step N and the path cycles with period at most N. A deterministic finite counterexample would refute it; the counting argument leaves no such system.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Definite rules means the next state is a function of the current state alone.

The bound applies to the eventual period, after a transient of length at most N.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: For every finite deterministic discrete system we enumerate, every orbit (from every possible state) becomes eventually periodic, and its eventual period is at most N, the total number of possible states of the system (and the transient plus period is also at most N).

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py builds, for each enumerated system, the complete transition map on its N global states and computes for every state the transient length and the eventual period from the functional graph (in-degree peeling to find cycle nodes, cycle walking for periods, vectorised relaxation for transients). It then counts orbits with period > N or transient + period > N. Families: 256 ECA x ring sizes 1..12 (3072 systems, 2,096,640 orbits), 4096 two-state two-colour Turing machines x cyclic tapes 1..5 (20,480 systems, 2,113,536 orbits), and x -> m x mod n for n = 2..200 (20,099 maps, 2,686,699 orbits). Total 43,651 systems and 6,896,875 orbits; run time about 4 s.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered: across all enumerated systems and all initial states, 100% of orbits satisfy period <= N and transient + period <= N (zero violations), where N is the exact number of distinct global states of the system.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered: at least one orbit of at least one enumerated system has eventual period > N, or never repeats within N + 1 steps (impossible to observe without a period > N, so equivalently a measured period exceeding N).

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: fraction of orbits with eventual period <= N and transient + period <= N

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Wolfram's 'system of limited size that involves discrete elements and follows definite rules' is read as a deterministic map f on a finite set of N global states, so 'definite rules' means the next state depends only on the current state. 'Eventually exhibit repetitive behavior' is read as: the orbit s, f(s), f(f(s)), ... is eventually periodic, with the eventual period (cycle length) at most N; the text's surrounding argument (p. 255) gives exactly this bound. Three concrete families of finite systems from the book's own repertoire are enumerated: the 256 elementary cellular automata on cyclic rings of n cells (N = 2^n), the 4096 two-state two-color Turing machines on cyclic tapes of n cells (N = 2 * n * 2^n: head state x head position x tape contents), and the modular multiplication maps x -> m x mod n (N = n). For every system every state is used as an initial condition, so the test is exhaustive within the enumerated sizes. The claim is a theorem (pigeonhole principle); the computation checks that the stated bound is never exceeded in these families and records how close observed periods come to it.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
All 256 elementary cellular automata on cyclic rings of n = 1..12 cells, all 2^n initial states (generated by analysis.py)

All 4096 two-state two-colour Turing machines on cyclic tapes of n = 1..5 cells, all initial configurations (generated by analysis.py)

Maps x -> m x mod n for n = 2..200 and m = 0..n-1, all initial residues (generated by analysis.py)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
The claim is a theorem (pigeonhole principle on a finite state set), so a finite enumeration can only fail to refute it; the enumeration here covers three concrete families exhaustively up to the stated sizes and finds the bound tight (period = N in degenerate 1-cell systems, period = N - 1 for x -> 3x mod 199).

Wolfram's bound is on the eventual period; the test also checks the slightly stronger transient + period <= N, which is what the pigeonhole argument actually gives, and it held in every orbit.

Systems whose next state depends on more than the current state (external input, randomness, unbounded memory) are outside the claim's scope and were not tested.
